articles.title: Pronouncing Law Latin
articles.content:
A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A. Kelly (who is emeritus in the English Department). It's called "Lawyers' Latin: Loquenda ut Vulgus?," and here's the introduction (though all 14 pages of the article are much worth reading):
In "Rex v. Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A. P. Herbert's "Misleading Cases"), Mr. Wick, an advocate making his first appearance in the High Court, tries out his textbook Latin before the Lord Chief Justice. The young advocate, attempting to apply for a writ of certiorari, asks for "a rule of neesee of kairtiorahree." The Lord Chief Justice pretends not to understand this or any other of Mr. Wick's Latin phrases. When ultra vires is rendered ooltrah weerayze, the Court interrupts: "Stop! Listen, Mr. Wick. The two groups of sounds last formed by you have no meaning for me, and I order you not to make use of them again."
Although the unfortunate Mr. Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:
It is not for me at my time of life to learn a new language; it is not for the King's judges to remodel their diction according to the whims of pedagogues or the habits of the Junior Bar. The bitter conclusion is, Mr. Wick, that you must go away and learn to pronounce the Latin tongue correctly, according to the immemorial practice of your profession.
According to the juristic apophthegm, Loquendum ut vulgus, sentiendum ut docti, one should "speak like the common people but understand like the learned." When it comes to legal Latin, lawyers have observed the first part of this advice in various ways. Traditionally, Latin in England and other European countries has not been spoken uniformly but has been pronounced according to the sounds of the vernacular or lingua vulgaris of each region. Nowadays, however, most lawyers must be classed with the vulgus in never having learned Latin, and so they tend to avoid it whenever possible. But when an expression is unavoidable, they give it what they consider to be the "most common" pronunciation, or they imitate the commons in acting according to whim rather than according to rule. The result is what we might charitably call an eclectic or ad hoc approach—we hear, for example, ADD HOCK, ODD HAWK, ADD HOKE, ODD OAK, and so on.
Four different but internally consistent systems of Latin pronunciation have been used in England and America, each entirely "correct" and defensible in theory and in practice. The following analysis is concerned more with showing how the four methods have been adapted to English tongues than with reflecting how each would be spoken by a "native" or purist. My aim, after tracing the vagaries of Latin pronunciation, is to offer some practical recommendations to English-speaking lawyers using Latin phrases….
For the lawyer who occasionally uses Latin words or phrases, I recommend that all expressions that have survived comfortably from an era when all Latin was pronounced in the English way—for example, et cetera—should continue to be pronounced as English, that is, in the English system of pronouncing Latin outlined above. But when Latin is cited as a foreign language, it should either be pronounced according to the system used by its author (if it is a literary citation) or according to any of the four systems outlined here that seems apt or convenient. Most often, no doubt, the system used will be the one learned in school.
But lawyers and legal educators should keep in mind the certainty of Herbert's Lord Chief Justice that such "hateful sounds" as "ooltrah weerayze" (for ultra vires) "will never proceed from the lips of an English judge, however many innocent boys are instructed to make them at school." Those who learned the Classical system need to be cautioned against trying to impose it upon all Latin expressions as if it were the only correct, or the most correct, way of pronouncing Latin. To do so would be to mistake the purpose of the scholars who resurrected it. It was intended only for the classics of the Golden Age of Latin, not for later Latin or for technical Latin terms or phrases brought into the various vernaculars in modern times
He labels the four methods "Classical (Ciceronian)," "Italian (Dantean)," "Continental (Chaucerian)," and "English (Shakespearean)," and discuss them further. He also cites a medieval source which I quite liked, at least with regard to pronunciation:
[T]he desire to appear wise among the foolish … is itself a kind of madness.
The post Pronouncing Law Latin appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: China Approved This Lung Cancer Drug. The FDA Is Making Americans Wait.
articles.content:
China approved a drug for some patients with advanced lung cancer in May 2024. American doctors still can't routinely offer it. On November 15, Summit Therapeutics announced that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had rejected its application to market the drug ivonescimab for patients whose cancer had progressed despite targeted treatment. Adding the drug to chemotherapy kept the cancer in check longer than chemotherapy alone, but the global trial didn't show that patients lived longer. According to Summit, the FDA wasn't convinced the delay justified making the drug available in the United States.
Some lung cancers grow because of a mutation in the gene for a protein called EGFR, short for "epidermal growth factor receptor." The mutation can leave the cell's growth signal stuck in the "on" position. Doctors can block that signal with a drug called Tagrisso. In one randomized trial, patients who started treatment with Tagrisso and chemotherapy lived a median of about 48 months, compared with about 38 months for those who took Tagrisso alone. Even with treatment, the cancer can start growing again.
Ivonescimab can slow the same type of lung cancer without blocking the faulty EGFR signal. It helps immune cells attack the cancer and interferes with the signals tumors use to grow blood vessels. In a global trial, patients who received ivonescimab with chemotherapy lived longer before their cancer worsened or they died than those who received chemotherapy alone. The trial didn't establish that patients lived longer overall. A separate Chinese trial did find a survival benefit.
In 2024, the FDA approved combining Rybrevant (amivantamab-vmjw) with chemotherapy for many of the same patients. That combination also kept the cancer in check longer than chemotherapy alone, but the evidence at the time didn't establish that patients lived longer. Why did a delay in tumor growth count then but fall short now?
Rybrevant's trial found that adding the drug to chemotherapy increased the frequency of rashes, nail problems, and infusion-related reactions. Ivonescimab studies have reported high blood pressure and protein in the urine. No trial has compared the drugs head-to-head, so we don't know which patients would tolerate either drug better overall. Even if ivonescimab never proves better than Rybrevant at extending life, patients and their doctors may weigh those risks differently. A second option could also give hospitals and insurers more room to negotiate on price.
The FDA may have good reasons for reaching different conclusions. The trials differed, and the drugs carry different risks. Many of these patients already have Rybrevant. But a patient who can't tolerate Rybrevant's side effects might be willing to accept the risks of ivonescimab. Another might choose Rybrevant because doctors have more experience with it. The FDA owes patients an explanation for treating the two drugs differently. With their doctors' help, patients should be free to decide which tradeoffs they're willing to make.
Congress passed the Right to Try Act in 2018 to give eligible patients with life-threatening illnesses a way to seek investigational drugs without asking the FDA to approve each request. But the FDA still decides whether the manufacturer can sell the drug. The law generally bars the agency from using a patient's outcome under Right to Try to delay or derail approval, but it allows an exception when the agency finds that the outcome is critical to judging the drug's safety. A manufacturer with years of work riding on an FDA decision may decide that supplying the drug outside a trial is too big a risk. Doctors and hospitals may have concerns of their own, and all should remain free to decline. The law's limited record shows how little waiving permission for individual requests can accomplish while the FDA still controls access to the market.
Congress can help by ending the FDA's authority to keep medicines off the market when informed adults are willing to use them. Ideally, Congress would abolish the agency and leave the evaluation of medicines to independent organizations. Researchers would still run trials. Doctors could explain the evidence to their patients, and manufacturers would still be held accountable for fraud and defective products. Adults could seek professional advice without the government making it a legal prerequisite to buying medicine.
If Congress isn't ready to go that far, it could start with "international drug reciprocity." When a foreign regulator that meets clear scientific review standards approves a drug, Congress could allow U.S. sales for the same use without requiring the manufacturer to undergo a second full approval process. Australia, New Zealand, Switzerland, and Israel already have ways to rely on foreign drug reviews or approvals without repeating the entire review. European Union members can recognize one another's drug approvals through a mutual recognition procedure. Manufacturers should clearly state on the label that the FDA hasn't approved the drug and identify the foreign agency that did. The same principle could apply to medicines that qualified regulators already allow people to buy without a prescription. Whether China's approval of ivonescimab would qualify would depend on the standards Congress sets. But when a foreign review meets those standards, why make American patients wait for Washington to repeat the work?
A patient whose lung cancer is growing again may be willing to try a drug that could keep it in check, even without proof it will extend their life. If they understand the risks and their doctor and the drugmaker are willing to help, Washington should get out of the way. The FDA can wait for more evidence. The patient may not have that luxury.
The post China Approved This Lung Cancer Drug. The FDA Is Making Americans Wait. appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Get Government Out of Air Traffic Control
articles.content:
The tottering nature of the U.S. air traffic control (ATC) system was highlighted again last week when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a "ground stop," halting flights across the country because of technical issues. The government is attributing the problem to equipment problems, which is believable for a long-obsolete, government-run system undergoing piecemeal modernization. In fact, the FAA had been warned that disruptions were likely. After repeated problems, sometimes caused by government shutdowns, it's time to point out once more that the U.S. should follow the lead of other countries and strip politicians of responsibility for something as important as air traffic control.
According to the FAA, last Friday, "the FAA's legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds. This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds."
The agency went on to deny that its ongoing efforts to upgrade the aging system are at fault, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy added that the problem occurred while L3Harris, a government contractor, "was replacing an old copper wire, which by the way, was going to be discontinued," and when a recently replaced router was turned back on, it flooded the system with data.
The ground stop isn't really a surprise. Air traffic control in the U.S. has stuttered in the past, most recently when last year's government shutdown left many federal workers laboring for delayed paychecks—and some air traffic controllers calling in sick. In 2023, a technical glitch in the system caused the delay and cancellation of thousands of flights. The creaky system has caused worries for years, inspiring modernization efforts. Just two weeks ago, Duffy boasted that the FAA is finally retiring 1980s-era floppy disks. But the upgrade program also causes concerns.
"We agree with the need to significantly accelerate the modernization of these ATC systems and applaud FAA's initial progress. However, in the interest of expediency, FAA is introducing additional risk," the Government Accountability Office (GAO) warned just two months ago. "In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions. The net effect could be that air traffic controllers are forced to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, or worse—safety incidents."
Unfortunately, government isn't good at slow and steady upgrades either. In 2005, the GAO cautioned that "the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) multibillion-dollar effort to modernize the nation's air traffic control (ATC) system has suffered from cost, schedule, and/or performance shortfalls in its system acquisitions for more than two decades and has been on our list of high risk programs since 1995."
And here we are. After decades of increasingly serious glitches, warnings, and ambitious upgrade plans, the air traffic control system still teeters on the edge of failure, and it just tipped over the edge—although temporarily. There must be a better way. In fact, there is.
"Today, roughly 100 countries receive their air traffic control services from user-funded utilities. Australia, Canada, Germany, and the U.K. all have newer, more-advanced technology than our Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and all of them are self-funded and independent of government budgets," Robert Poole of the Reason Foundation, which publishes Reason, wrote last November.
Poole and his colleagues have worked on the ATC issue for years, calling repeatedly for depoliticization and more private sector involvement. In July of this year, industry consultant John Kefaliotis wrote for the Reason Foundation that "Canada provides a working model of a successful transition from a tax-funded air traffic control system chronically short of adequate revenue and long-term financing to a sustainable, adaptable non-profit commercial structure capable of continuous modernization."
Hoover Institution research fellow David R. Henderson, a former adviser to the Reagan administration, agrees with that suggestion. He points out that the then-financially strapped Canadian government divested itself of ATC responsibilities in the 1990s. "In 1996, partly to save money and partly to improve air navigation, the feds sold the system to a private nonprofit company called Nav Canada," he noted after the 2023 U.S. ATC outage. "Almost immediately, Nav Canada acted to upgrade technology. How has Nav Canada performed? Very well."
Henderson pointed to a Reason Foundation study that found "Nav Canada has speeded up modernization, dramatically increased efficiency and productivity, and cut user fees by one-third."
Chris Edwards of the Cato Institute also likes that model. In 2024, he emphasized that "the privatized Canadian system has won numerous international awards and is a leader in many technologies. Canada and Europe are ahead of us, for example, on remote or digital towers, which surround runways with cameras and sensors to feed large video screens in control buildings."
Various flavors of ATC privatization have been on the table before. The Reagan administration considered the idea, and the Clinton administration floated a proposal for spinning it off into a user-funded corporation. Under the first Trump administration, then-House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Bill Shuster (R–Penn.) pushed for a Canadian-style ATC system separate from the government. He dropped it under pressure from entrenched interests.
"Despite an unprecedented level of support for this legislation—from bipartisan lawmakers, industry, and conservative groups and labor groups alike—some of my own colleagues refused to support shrinking the federal government by 35,000 employees, cutting taxes, and stopping wasteful spending," Shuster said at the time. He left Congress in 2019, though he continues to favor privatization.
Shuster's failed effort was the last serious attempt to reform air traffic control rather than prop up the decaying government scheme. After last week's ground stop, Duffy asked for an additional $50 billion to, hopefully, get the long-delayed modernization effort completed.
Maybe the U.S. government will finally succeed at making government a competent manager of air traffic control—a sensitive responsibility over which other governments have surrendered, one after another. More likely, we're in for repeated delays, cancellations, and mass disruptions as the government air traffic control system deteriorates until change is forced on resistant politicians.
The post Get Government Out of Air Traffic Control appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.content:
11/18/1811: Justice Gabriel Duvall takes judicial oath. Professor David P. Currie said that an "impartial examination of Duvall's performance reveals to even the uninitiated observer that he achieved an enviable standard of insignificance against which all other justices must be measured."

articles.title: Brickbat: Watch Where You Point That
articles.content:
District of Columbia police arrested William Clark for pointing a finger like a gun at National Guard troops near the White House. According to court documents, Clark was holding a cellphone in one hand while making a shooting gesture with the other. National Guard members detained him until D.C. police arrived and arrested him on charges of making threats in a menacing manner and assaulting a police officer. Prosecutors subsequently reduced the case to a misdemeanor charge of assault or threatened assault in a menacing manner.

The post Brickbat: Watch Where You Point That appeared first on Reason Magazine.
